atmosphere.source_sentence: Figure 3 shows the thermogravimetric analysis of the maleyl amide polymer stabilizers at a heating rate of $1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C / m m }$in air.

characterizations.result_summary: Thermal stability of three maleyl amide polymer stabilizers was measured, with melamine amide polymer showing highest stability, followed by p-phenylenediamine polymer, then m-phenylenediamine amide polymer.

evidence.source_sentence: Figure 3 shows the thermogravimetric analysis of the maleyl amide polymer stabilizers at a heating rate of $1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C / m m }$in air. The melamine amide polymer exhibits the highest thermal stability, since its decomposition starts at ${ \approx } 2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$and gradual degradation occurs up to $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ;$then complete decomposition takes place up to $4 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$The thermal stability of the p-phenylenediamine polymer is lower than that of the melamine one, since the decomposition begins at ${ \approx } 1 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$and after $2 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$the complete degradation occurs. The least thermally stable amide polymer is that of m-phenylenediamine, as shown in Fig. 3.
FIG. 3. Thermogravimetric analysis of some maleyl amide polymers in air, at a heating rate of 108C/min.

characterizations.result_summary: Weight loss of nonstabilized PVC and PVC stabilized with maleyl amide polymers was measured, with stabilized PVC showing lower weight loss at 320°C.
